summary: ExMonitor is a training simulator for crew health on long missions. A phone becomes a pretend body sensor; a laptop becomes the console with a live heart trace, five vital cards and a radiation dose bar. A deterministic rules engine marks every reading normal, watch or critical, and can raise a crew alert that every connected console must acknowledge. A language model runs entirely in the browser (or against a local Ollama server) so the assistant still answers offline. A written action-card mode needs no model at all. One button, Start Demo, runs the whole story on a single device in about 40 seconds.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ExMonitor is a browser-based crew health console for astronaut-medical training. A phone or second screen becomes a simulated body sensor; a laptop becomes the console. The console shows a live ECG trace, five vital cards (heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, skin-conductance stress and radiation dose rate) and a radiation bar scaled to a 600 mSv career limit.

HOW IT WORKS

- The sensor page generates realistic signals and streams eight frames per second.

- One telemetry provider validates and stores every frame, so every screen agrees.

- A deterministic rules engine classifies each reading as normal, watch or critical and returns a hazard, a recommended action and a short guidance label. It answers instantly and never depends on the AI.

- Critical readings can raise a crew alert. The sender sees a compact panel; every other console shows a full-screen alert until that crew member acknowledges it. The sender can cancel it everywhere.

- The assistant has two modes (Doctor mode attaches the current readings; Assistant mode is plain chat) and three sources: a model running on the device through WebLLM and WebGPU, a model the user already runs with Ollama, or No AI, which uses the written action cards and needs no download.

WHY IT IS USEFUL

The demo runs on one laptop with no second device, no camera and no network: Start Demo cycles rest, exercise, low oxygen, radiation storm and recovery in about 40 seconds and raises the alert during low oxygen. That makes it usable in a classroom, a hackathon booth or a remote location.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, WebLLM with WebGPU, the Web Audio API, WebSocket, BroadcastChannel, a PWA service worker, a zero-dependency Node.js launcher, Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects, and the qrcode package. The download page offers twelve ZIPs (three AI models plus No AI, on Windows, macOS and Linux).

CREATIVITY

The project combines three things that are usually separate: a simulated sensor, a deterministic safety net, and an optional AI that runs on the device. The AI sits above the rules, never below them, so the safety path still works when the model is missing or wrong. The one-tap demo removes every setup step.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Honesty and safety came first: all readings are simulated and the app says so. The thresholds are teaching values, not flight rules. We removed every NASA document number we could not verify; the only NASA figure left is the 600 mSv career dose limit from NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1, Revision C. The project is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA. Offline use, low-end hardware and privacy were also considered: no account, no cloud, no prompt leaves the device, and No AI works on any device.

AI DISCLOSURE

Most of the code and copy were produced in a pair-programming loop between the human author and an AI coding agent (OpenCode). The author chose the direction, reviewed every change, and ran the build and the app. No AI-generated images, audio or video are included. Full licences are in CREDITS.md.
dataRefs: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1, Revision C — Space Permissible Exposure Limits (600 mSv career limit)
